title: Merrick Ancestral Land
summary: Merrick and Merikoke homelands are remembered around the Hempstead plains, south shore bays, creeks, meadows, shellfish waters, planting grounds, and travel routes. The name appears in colonial and later sources in several spellings, including Merrick, Meroke, Merikoke, Mericoke, Merriack, Merricock, and Mercock.
address_label: Broad Merrick / Freeport / Bellmore / Hempstead Plains and south shore wetland landscape, Nassau County, NY
ancestral_territory_note: Primary Merrick ancestral land record for related south shore and Hempstead Plains related south shore and Hempstead Plains entries.
why_this_matters: Merrick Ancestral Land presents Nassau County's south shore as Native homeland: a place of language, plains, creeks, shellfish waters, travel routes, diplomacy, and continuing memory. The Merrick/Meroke references also shows that colonial land loss was contested. Native leaders and communities remained active in negotiations, legal challenges, kinship networks, and public memory long after early deeds were written.
introduction_title: Merrick / Merikoke People And South Shore Homelands
introduction_content: Historian John A. Strong's critique of the popular "thirteen tribes" list cautions against turning deed language into an artificial map of fixed tribes. Merrick is better understood as a place-based community name: land and water gave Europeans a name to write down, while Indigenous life itself crossed later town lines through kinship, diplomacy, work, and movement. Merrick/Merikoke history overlaps with Massapequa, Rockaway, Canarsie, Secatogue, Matinecock, and other western Long Island Native histories. The name keeps people visible where modern maps often remember only roads, towns, and property lines.
history_content:
Early land papers connect Merrick/Mericock forms with the 1643 Hempstead land transaction involving Native representatives associated with Massapequa, Merrick, and Rockaway communities and English purchasers Robert Fordham and John Carman. The named references include Tackapousha and other representatives whose names are preserved on the Merrick People in Early Land Records page.

Later records show that these transactions did not settle the meaning of land, payment, or authority. A 1656 Dutch treaty context involving Adam (Achitteronose) included Meracock/Merrick among western Long Island allied communities. In 1657, Native representatives connected with the Merrick villages joined a Hempstead meeting with Tackapousha, Wyandanch, Cockenoe, Mangwobe, and town officials to revisit land boundaries and claims. In 1675, Tackapousha publicly challenged Hempstead use of Mercock land by stating that it had not been paid for.

These records are not simply sale documents. They show diplomacy, pressure, translation, boundary disputes, and Native legal resistance during a period when colonial governments were turning Native homelands into English town land.
translation_content: Merrick and Merricock are connected with an Algonquian place-name meaning related to bare land, barren land, or plain. The interpretation fits the Hempstead Plains, a large open grassland remembered in Native and colonial geography. Because written spellings came through English and Dutch record keepers, these forms are best read as a references rather than a single final spelling. Recorded forms include Merriack, Merioke, Meracock, Moroke, Mericoke, Mericock, Merricock, Marrocock, Mercock, Merikoke, and Meroke.
preservation_title: Public Memory And Care For Sensitive Places
preservation_content:
Some Merrick-Freeport-area histories involve village places, shell deposits, family landscapes, and archaeological traces that should not be mapped for public visitation. The history shares the broader Native history of the landscape while protecting culturally sensitive places, private property, and archaeological locations.

The missing New York State Meroke marker in Merrick is one reminder that public memory can appear, disappear, and be restored through careful education. Freeport's scheduled 2026 Living Conduit - Indigenous History and Present Day exhibition is a modern acknowledgment point connecting On This Site landscapes with contemporary Indigenous presence. [1. John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.; SNUUC On This Site and Portrait Show pre-publicity draft; SNUUC On This Site exhibition project outline.]
artifacts_content: Local history and archaeology sources describe shell deposits, tools, and other material evidence in the broader south shore creek-and-meadow landscape, including nineteenth-century accounts from the Milburn Creek/Hick's Neck area. These records point to long Indigenous use of estuary resources, shellfish waters, nearby uplands, and south shore travel routes. Burial information, private findspots, and directions for artifact collecting are not included here. [1. The Illustrated Story of Baldwin Long Island, N.Y.; Baldwin: Our Heritage (1976); James Truex, ed., The Second Coastal Archaeological Reader: 1900 to the Present.]
colonial_description_content: Contact-period records tied to Merrick/Mericock include the December 13, 1643 Hempstead deed, the March 12, 1656 Dutch treaty context involving western Long Island allied communities, the July 4, 1657 Hempstead conference, Tackapousha's 1675 challenge over unpaid Mercock land, and Reverend Azariah Horton's 1742 mission visits. These records show diplomacy, translation, religious pressure, land conflict, and Native legal resistance, not a simple one-time transfer of land. [1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.; Long Island Historical Journal discussion of Reverend Azariah Horton's 1742 mission journal.]
land_loss_content: For Merrick people and neighboring Native communities, land loss unfolded through deed making, town expansion, disputed payments, forced movement, changing access to meadows and waterways, and colonial legal systems that narrowed Native land rights over time. Merrick history is best understood as part of a wider western Long Island story of survival, adaptation, kinship, and continued Native presence after dispossession.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The Hempstead Plains and Merrick/Freeport/Bellmore south-shore landscape, including the Long Beach barrier and western Hempstead Bay islands. The line toward Massapequa and Rockaway follows a generalized nearest-landscape partition rather than a claimed historical border.
